title: Is it true that games made with generative AI don't sell?
author: FilipeDM
selftext: Not long ago, Steam hosted an event dedicated to games developed using generative AI, and the reception was quite negative. A large portion of the public still seems to have a strong aversion to AI-generated content, often associating this type of production with what is commonly called “AI slop.” I wanted to confirm whether this is actually true.

comments.author: djmisterjon
comments.body:
The main problem is that everyone is being put in the same boat.

It’s a bit like what happened to restaurants when the food industry arrived. Some started reheating industrial products in the microwave, while others learned to use industrial resources intelligently while still maintaining quality.

Buying dried parsley instead of growing it yourself doesn’t turn a restaurant into a fast-food joint. Yet for a while, simply using industrial ingredients was enough to put a restaurant in the same category as McDonald’s.

The same thing is happening to creators. You can do 90% of the work yourself, but the moment you use these mathematical models to improve your art, code, or tools, you can end up being lumped together with people generating one game a day from a simple prompt and no care about quality and gameplay.

I’ve been developing a JRPG for \~10 years. I showed on a Discord how my art has evolved over the years. I can’t even tell you how much hate I received for it from designer !

replies.author: Alternative-Bread411
replies.body:
This is really well put! “AI-assisted” is just too broad a term.

Based on your analogy, I also wonder if things will settle over time as people become more informed about AI use and vote with their wallets. It’ll become easier for rfolk to distinguish exploitative, lazy AI use, or using it purely because it’s cheap, from credible use that contributes to the craftsmanship of a great product.

I think the same analogy applies to polyester in clothing, an industrial material that enabled a flood of cheap products, but can also be used intelligently in well-made clothing. Some consumers in droves take a genuine interest in how polyester is used in products.

Ultimately, give it a few years and I strongly believe things will settle down. When that time comes we'll all start thinking more clearly.

comments.author: SushiMasterPro
comments.body:
**Generative AI is already used in games at big studios, including ones you wouldn't expect**. I don't go to details here it would be long post. 

So AI isn't just a tool for small low-effort studios anymore.

**The main change is how many games come out.** AI coding tools made it much faster and cheaper to ship a game, and release numbers have jumped:

**iOS**

* \~600k new apps in 2025 (+30%), then \~560k in H1 2026 alone, so on pace for about 2x.
* Mobile game launches up 118% year over year.
* Downloads only grew 2%. More games are competing for the same players.

**Android**

* Mobile game launches up 73% year over year.
* Studios releasing their first game up 82%.
* Between Dec 2025 and Feb 2026, game releases jumped 77%, but games making over $20k grew only 14%.
* \~97% of new games still get under 1,000 downloads.

**Steam**

* \~14.5k games released in 2023, \~19k in 2024, \~20k in 2025.
* About 1 in 3 new releases now discloses AI use, up from almost none in 2023.
* 60–90% of the recent growth in releases comes from AI-flagged games.

**Result:** marketing is harder for everyone, including indie games made with no AI at all. More releases means more competition for visibility, wishlists and players' attention.

comments.author: Fun_Bumblebee_3978
comments.body:
I'll be honest, I took this one personally. Not because the post is wrong about the numbers, but because of the story people have built around them.

Yes, the reception was negative. Yes, "AI slop" exists, and nobody hates a lazy, generic game more than the people who actually love games. But somewhere along the way, a tool became a verdict. The moment a game is associated with AI, a lot of players stop looking at the game and start looking for a reason to reject it.

Here's the irony: AI has been part of game development for decades. The xenomorph in Alien: Isolation, which everyone rightly praises, is AI. Pathfinding, procedural terrain, upscaling, animation blending, code assistants, texture tools: modern studios, big and small, already use AI throughout their pipelines. The difference is that when a billion-dollar company does it, it's called "innovation." When a solo dev does it, it's called "slop."

And let's talk about those billion-dollar companies for a second. They spend fortunes on games built from the same template, recycled year after year, sold at $60, $70, even $90, sometimes running on the bones of engines that are nearly two decades old. Many of those games are designed less to be enjoyed and more to be farmed: battle passes, grind loops, microtransactions dressed up as content. Yet those studios rarely get the same outrage. The loudest voices against "AI games" are often defending the very industry that has been squeezing them the hardest.

I'm a full-time developer, working alone on an MMO. Before these tools, I was digging a mountain with a shovel. Today I have an excavator. The mountain is still just as big. The vision, the design, the systems, the late nights, the bugs at 3 AM, the decisions about what the game should feel like: that's still me. AI didn't replace my creativity. It removed the wall that was standing between my ideas and the screen.

That's the part people miss. Behind many of these "AI games" there isn't a faceless corporation cutting costs. There's a gamer who grew up dreaming of making the game they always wanted to play, and who finally has the tools to try. It's not about replacing artists. It's about letting people who were never given a studio, a budget, or a team finally build something.

Rejecting a game because of the tools used to make it is like rejecting a house because the builder used a power drill instead of a hand crank. Judge the house. Is it solid? Is it beautiful? Would you want to live in it? That's the only question that matters.

And on that point, I actually agree with the post completely: the easier it becomes to make a game, the less impressive it is to simply make one. The value moves to making something people genuinely want to play. That's a good thing. It raises the bar for everyone, AI or not. Bad games will still be bad games. Great games will still find their players.

So all I'm asking is this: don't let a label do your thinking for you. Play the game, then judge it. Time has a way of settling these arguments, and I believe that in a few years, "made with AI" will sound as strange as "made with a computer."

Until then, some of us will keep building. Not to cash in on a trend, but because we've wanted to do this our whole lives.

comments.body:
I am not against AI, I know that AI is maybe most powerful tool we have ever made. And every developement company is using it as part of their workflow. That said, it very difficoult if not impossible to make fully AI generated game and to be good, have complex mechanics, good art that is consistent, animations, vfx, persect sound. It need touch of a human. I am learning UE5 engine for 6 months now. And every day I make hundreds of small design or gameplay decision AI would never be able to make or to see. Simply because it doesn't have eyes, feelings, 35 years of gaming experience...

Not to mention tech debt that I am 1000% sure 90% of people will have down the line 6 months in developement and thousands of hours later. 

AI in hands of professional dev can be powerful tool, and I believein next couple of years we will have influx of many good games just because many devs got fired and realized they can join forces with artist or two and make AA games themselves. 

But we are still not at point of me or people with even less experience can just make a game with AI and without otevious knowledge or will to learn. That is why I learn C++, UE5.8 and trying to make game I would love to play. With focus off feeling, something I am sure AI can't make at least for couple of years. 

Ps. I KNOW 2 people who vibe code their games brute forcing with Astra and its really bad.

comments.author: virt111
comments.body:
Pure asset flip slop don't sell well. But games where the AI is used so well that it isn't blatantly obvious do sell. For example I've done the splash screen with the help of AI. I'm not gonna post it here though. I basically first generated an image in some image generator software, then I passed it through another LLM that made a pixel art version of it. Then I opened it in photoshop and cleaned it up and tweaked a bit. Then I made a 2d Parallax kinda layering on it and created a "cutscene" like splash screen for my game. No one knows it's AI. But then again I did spend hours on it, so it wasn't just "one prompt and into production".

I also use AI for color scheme stuff. It's great that I can describe a picture with some kinda feel and the AI plops out a cool picture of the setting or scene. Then I just pick the colors from the screen to create my own art and graphics.
